One focuses on social variation and the other on the workings of the mind.

ling-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: The Procedure for Analyzing Language Data
explain: So far we have learned sounds, words, sentences, meaning, and change and variation step by step. This lesson ties them into a single line. When a linguist is given data from an unfamiliar language, there is a basic procedure they go through. The capstone in the final lesson is a task of using this procedure yourself.

The procedure can be organized into five steps. (1) Gather and organize the data. (2) Find recurring patterns. (3) Propose a rule that explains the patterns as a hypothesis. (4) Check whether the hypothesis makes correct predictions about new data. (5) Revise the hypothesis if a counterexample appears. The simpler a hypothesis is, the better, but simplicity is not the same as correctness.

For sound data there are two tools. One is the **minimal pair**: if there is a pair of words that differ in only one sound and differ in meaning, the two sounds are different phonemes. The other is **complementary distribution**: if two sounds appear only in different environments, do not overlap, and are phonetically close, they are likely to be two **allophones** of one phoneme. For example, suppose a hypothetical language has the words tama, tomu, and tuka as well as chiba and chini. [t] appears only before a, o, and u, and [ch] only before i, so their environments do not overlap, and the two can be interpreted as allophones of one phoneme.

In morphological data, we compare words and look for parts that change consistently. For example, if ona means "book" and ona-ki means "books", -ki is likely an affix expressing the plural. In the same way, if lap means "reads" and lap-ta means "read" (past), we assume -ta is a past affix. In syntactic data, we compare the order of subject, object, and verb and the position of affixes to determine word order.

Recall the experience of working through each area with Korean, English, and Latin data. In phonology there were features and the ordering of rules; in morphology, allomorphs and productivity; in syntax, constituents and movement constraints; in semantics, truth conditions and scope; in pragmatics, implicature and presupposition; in history, correspondence and reconstruction; and in society, the quantification of variation. Analyzing an unfamiliar language is a matter of taking these tools out where they are needed.

The limits must also be made clear. When data are few, several different analyses may all fit the data. This is called underdetermination. Also, no conclusion can be drawn about environments absent from the data. For example, if there is no example of a sound appearing at the beginning of a word, we cannot assert whether it can or cannot occur word-initially. A good analysis states both what it is sure of and what it is not sure of.

examples.title: Judging Whether Sounds Are Allophones or Separate Phonemes
body: Condition: Data from a hypothetical language: pasa, pita, aba, ubi. p appears at the beginning of a word, and b only between vowels.
Step 1: Look for minimal pairs. There is no pair of words in the data that differ only in p and b and differ in meaning.

Step 2: Look at distribution. p is word-initial and b is between vowels, so the environments do not overlap (complementary distribution). Both sounds are produced at the lips, so they are also phonetically close.
Interpretation: We propose the hypothesis that p and b are allophones of one phoneme. However, since the data are few, it should be tested with more words.

examples.title: Inferring the Meaning of Affixes and Word Order
body: Condition: In a hypothetical language, Mira ona lap means "Mira reads the book," and Mira ona-ki lap-ta means "Mira read the books." Mira is a person's name.

Step 1: Comparing the two sentences, the only differences are -ki attached to ona and -ta attached to lap, and the differences in meaning are "plural" and "past." We infer that -ki is plural and -ta is past.
Step 2: The word order is name (subject) - ona (object) - lap (verb).
Interpretation: The word order appears to be subject - object - verb, and affixes attach after the root. With this hypothesis, we can also predict the meaning of a new sentence such as "Mira lap-ta."

checks.prompt: Arrange in order the procedure for analyzing data from an unfamiliar language.
checks.hint: Find patterns before setting up rules, and testing is possible only once there is a hypothesis.
checks.explanation: The cycle of organizing, patterns, hypothesis, testing, and revision is the basic framework of analysis.
items: Find patterns such as minimal pairs and distribution
Propose a rule that explains the patterns as a hypothesis
Test the hypothesis's predictions with new data
Revise the hypothesis if a counterexample appears

checks.prompt: A hypothetical language has the words pasa, pita, pona, aba, ubi, and obo, all with different meanings. p appears at the beginning of a word, and b only between vowels. Which is the most suitable interpretation?
checks.hint: See whether there is a pair of words that differ in only two sounds and split in meaning, and whether the environments where the two sounds appear overlap.
checks.explanation: There are no minimal pairs and the distribution is complementary, so an allophone hypothesis is possible. But because the data are few, it must be stated as a hypothesis.
options: p and b are separate phonemes, because there are minimal pairs
p and b are in complementary distribution with non-overlapping environments, so they are likely two allophones of one phoneme
p and b are not consonants
Nothing can be said from the data

checks.prompt: In a hypothetical language, ona means "book," ona-ki "books," lap "reads," and lap-ta "read." How many morphemes in all does the sentence Mira ona-ki lap-ta ("Mira read the books") contain?
checks.hint: Count Mira, ona, ki, lap, and ta each as a morpheme.
checks.explanation: Mira, ona, -ki, lap, -ta: five.

checks.prompt: The books read by three students are {a, b} for Mina, {b} for Jun, and {b, c} for Seoyun. When "There is a book that every student read" (a > every) is true, which is correct about "Every student read a book" (every > a)?
checks.hint: If there is a book that everyone read together, think about whether each student has a book they read.
checks.explanation: If a > every is true, every > a is necessarily true. The converse does not hold.
options: The every > a interpretation is false
It cannot be judged from the data
The two interpretations contradict each other
The every > a interpretation is also true. If there is a book b that everyone read, each student also has a book they read

checks.prompt: There are the correspondences Latin pater - English father, tres - three, cornu - horn. If this correspondence is a rule, what is the initial sound letter of the English word corresponding to Latin piscis (fish)?
checks.hint: Check from pater - father which sound Latin p is paired with in English.
checks.explanation: Latin p corresponds to English f, so it is the f of English fish.

ling-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Analyzing a Corpus of Sena (Hypothetical)
explain: The capstone task is to analyze a small body of data from a language you have never seen. The **Sena language** used here is a hypothetical language made for practice and has no relation to any real language. From the data below alone, you propose hypotheses about rules of phonology, morphology, and syntax, and write a report stating how far you can be confident in those hypotheses.

Word list (Sena - meaning):
- pasa - house
- pita - water
- aba - road
- ubi - fire
- tuka - bird
- kuka - tree
- taki - stone
- kasu - child
- mira - see
- sumi - drink

Sentence data (Sena - meaning):
1. kasu tuka mira. - The child sees a bird.
2. kasu-ni pita sumi. - The children drink water.
3. kasu kuka-ni mira-ra. - The child saw trees.
4. kasu-ni ubi mira-ra. - The children saw a fire.
5. kasu pita sumi-ra. - The child drank water.

The analysis proceeds in three layers. Phonology: examine pairs of similar sounds by minimal pairs and distribution. For example, tuka and kuka differ only in the first sound, showing that t and k are separate phonemes. For p and b, make a table of the environments where they appear. Morphology: in sentences 2 to 5, find the meaning of the repeated -ni and -ra and what they attach to. Syntax: check the order of subject, object, and verb and whether there is a marker that marks the object.

The report is written in the following frame. (1) The scope of the data. (2) Phonological hypotheses and evidence. (3) Morphological hypotheses and evidence. (4) Syntactic hypotheses and evidence. (5) One new sentence predicted by the hypotheses and its meaning. (6) What the data let you be sure of and what they do not. Present evidence by directly citing words or sentence numbers.

There are three criteria for self-checking. Does the hypothesis fit all the data? Is the evidence tied to specific examples in the data? Have you avoided carelessly generalizing to environments absent from the data? This task is not graded; a checklist is used instead of a model answer. After finishing, look for the weak points of your own hypotheses and try revising them.

Let us point out the limits and ethics. Ten words and five sentences are a very small body of data, so there may be other analyses that fit the same data. When researching real languages, especially minority languages, the consent and cooperation of the speakers and the community are essential, and a researcher must not take and use data arbitrarily. Because this task uses a hypothetical language, we can set this concern aside and concentrate only on the analytic procedure.

examples.title: Making a Distribution Table for p and b
body: Condition: The words in the data that contain p or b are pasa, pita, aba, and ubi.
Step 1: Write down the positions. In pasa and pita, p is word-initial; in aba and ubi, b is between two vowels.
Step 2: Compare the environments. p appears only at the beginning of a word and b only between vowels, so they do not overlap. There are also no minimal pairs.
Interpretation: Because the distribution is complementary, we hypothesize that p and b are allophones of one phoneme. However, whether b can occur at the beginning of a word is not in the data.

examples.title: Extracting Affixes and Word Order
body: Condition: Compare sentence 2, kasu-ni pita sumi., and sentence 5, kasu pita sumi-ra.

Step 1: When -ni is attached to kasu, the meaning becomes "children," and when -ra is attached to sumi, it becomes "drank." We hypothesize that -ni is a plural attached to nouns and -ra is a past attached to verbs. The same affixes repeat in sentences 3 and 4.
Step 2: Looking at the order of words, in sentences 1 to 5 it is subject, object, verb. No separate marker attached to the object appears in the data.

Interpretation: The word order appears to be subject - object - verb, and affixes attach after the root. With this hypothesis, kasu-ni pasa mira-ra can be predicted to mean "The children saw a house."

checks.prompt: Match each hypothesis obtained from the Sena data with its evidence.
checks.hint: Find in the data which words or sentences serve as evidence for each hypothesis.
checks.explanation: Minimal pairs are evidence for a phonemic contrast, complementary distribution for allophones, and repeated affixes for morphological hypotheses.
pairs: t and k are separate phonemes
tuka (bird) and kuka (tree) differ only in the first sound
p and b are allophones of one phoneme
p appears only at the beginning of a word and b only between vowels
When kasu changes to kasu-ni, "child" becomes "children"
When sumi changes to sumi-ra, "drink" becomes "drank"

checks.prompt: How many morphemes are there in all in sentence 3, "kasu kuka-ni mira-ra"?
checks.hint: Count kasu, kuka, -ni, mira, and -ra one by one.
checks.explanation: Three roots, kasu, kuka, and mira, and two affixes, -ni and -ra: 5 in all.

checks.prompt: What cannot be concluded from this corpus alone?
checks.hint: Distinguish the environments that appear in the data from those that do not.
checks.explanation: b appeared only between vowels and there is no word-initial b in the data, so whether it is possible cannot be asserted.
options: That the word order appears to be subject - object - verb
That -ni appears to be a plural marker attached to nouns
Whether b can occur at the beginning of a word

checks.prompt: Summarize in 3 to 5 sentences the hypotheses set up from the Sena data, in terms of word order, affixes, and sounds.
checks.hint: Write one sentence each in the order word order, affixes, sounds, and add the limits at the end.
checks.explanation: A clear summary makes the evidence in the report clear.
checks.model: The word order of Sena appears to be subject, object, verb, and the data have no separate marker for the object. The affix -ni attaches to nouns to express the plural and -ra attaches to verbs to express the past, and both attach after the root. In sounds, the contrast between tuka and kuka shows that t and k are separate phonemes, while p and b show complementary distribution, with p at the beginning of a word and b only between vowels, so they may be allophones of one phoneme. However, the data are small, so there are parts that cannot be settled.

checks.prompt: Capstone task: Following the frame (1) to (6) above, write an analysis report on the Sena data. Present hypotheses and evidence for phonology (distribution table), morphology (the meaning and position of affixes), and syntax (word order) by sentence number, predict one new sentence, and write at least 400 characters distinguishing what the data let you be sure of from what they do not.
checks.hint: Fill in the frame (1) to (6) in turn, and cite words or sentence numbers directly as evidence.
checks.explanation: This task is not graded. Use the checklist to improve it yourself.
checklist: I stated the scope of the data (10 words, 5 sentences)
I gave minimal pairs or a distribution table as evidence for the phonological hypothesis
I supported the meaning and position of the affixes -ni and -ra by sentence number
I presented a word-order hypothesis and a prediction for one new sentence
I distinguished what the data let me be sure of from what they do not
